title: Why Jason Cohen ignored "that's how it's done" and sold to the Enterprise at Smart Bear
summary: Jason Cohen recounts how Smart Bear broke every conventional rule for selling to enterprises (silly name, no traditional sales force, slide-free demos, amateur design, human voice) and still reached millions in revenue. His point: conventional wisdom describes what works for most, but you can choose your own way if you go in eyes open and accept the harder road.

principles.text: Conventional wisdom describes how most successful companies do it; it isn't wrong, but it isn't the only way.
principles.quote: "They" are in fact describing the way most *successful* companies sell to The Enterprise. Nothing wrong with "tried and true."

principles.text: Smart Bear sold to the Enterprise while breaking the usual rules: odd name, no sales force, slide-free demos, human voice.
principles.quote: Oops. I accidentally went and did *all* that at Smart Bear, and only had millions of dollars of revenue to show for it. Largely from The Enterprise.

principles.text: If the tried-and-true path doesn't fit who you are, don't force it; compete with big companies instead of imitating them.
principles.quote: Unless tried and true doesn't happen to jibe with you.

principles.text: Going unconventional is often not strategy but inability to do it the standard way; follow your own constraints.
principles.quote: I wasn't trying to be "disruptive" or "innovative" or a "maverick." I just *couldn't do it*.

principles.text: Ignoring convention makes the road harder and removes your safety net, so go in eyes open; being different can be enough if for a good reason.
principles.quote: Once you buck "Their" wisdom, you can't rely on "Them" when you get yourself into an unusual pickle. You've exited the safe and well-travelled road.

principles.text: Don't let "it's not done that way" alone decide; maybe it should be done your way.
principles.quote: Don't let the "it's not done that way" people win on that basis alone.
